WHY THIS IS RECORDED RATHER THAN JUST FIXED: the post had already passed a verifier and an integration pass, and the error survived both, because both were checking compliance and structure rather than arithmetic. L009 RECURRED INSIDE THE IMPLEMENTATION PLAN ITSELF, caught by the Task 1 agent and corrected before Task 2 ran. The plan used `grep -c` for TWENTY-THREE count checks against files under dist/. Astro emits built HTML as effectively ONE LINE, so `grep -c` returns 1 whenever the pattern appears at all. THAT BREAKS IN BOTH DIRECTIONS: a check expecting 6 (for example the plan's `rto-faq-item` assertion) reads 1 and FALSE-FAILS a correct build, while a check expecting exactly 1 (for example `"@type":"Article"`) reads 1 and FALSE-PASSES a broken one. The defect spanned Tasks 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7. L009's recorded consequence is precisely the danger: 'the likely response to that false alarm is to fix correct work.' CORRECTED 2026-08-14 by the orchestrator: 23 dist/ count checks rewritten to `grep -o ... | wc -l`; 3 legitimate `grep -c` uses against MULTI-LINE SOURCE files left alone, since there the line count is the right metric; and a verification note added at the top of the plan's Global Constraints section so no later task reintroduces it. Plan re-verified dash-clean afterwards. WHY THIS IS RECORDED RATHER THAN PROMOTED AS A NEW LESSON: L009 already states the rule ('never mix grep -c and grep -o | wc -l in one piece of arithmetic; state which metric a threshold refers to'). What is new is the CONTEXT: the defect appeared in a planning artifact rather than in a verification run, where it would have been executed by five separate agents who each see only their own task and could not have noticed the pattern. A systemic check defect in a plan is worse than one in a script, because it is copied rather than run once.

(1) DELIVERY COST IS DISTANCE-DRIVEN and is the entire mechanism behind these figures (observed: $591.67 for 20 miles in Atlanta, amortizing to +$27/mo). A national average blends Los Angeles and Newark into a number that is wrong for everyone in Ohio: too high for a buyer near a depot, too low for one far from it. It averages away the only variable that matters. (2) IT IS A STEP DOWN FROM WHAT THE SITE ALREADY DOES. src/data/pricing.ts holds average starting prices for the containers SBD sells in the markets SBD serves, owner-confirmed, dated, with the 'your quote may be more or less' disclaimer. A national RTO blend would average in markets SBD does not serve, so it is LESS defensible than the existing pattern, not a safe fallback to it. (3) WORDING: 'call for the best price' implies negotiation and invites a haggle; the existing disclaimer sets expectations without promising a discount for phoning. THE CORRECT FALLBACK is the three-ZIP variance pull in T-094, which is smaller work and produces a market-grounded answer.

THE HONEST COMPARISON FRAME for the rental page, and it needs no third-party data. The owner's intended pitch is 'renting a container is more expensive than buying one'. THE FRAME THAT WORKS INSTEAD IS STRUCTURAL RATHER THAN PRICE-VERSUS-PRICE: rent for 24 months and you have made 24 payments and own nothing; rent-to-own for 24 months at a comparable payment and the container is yours. That is an arithmetic truth about the STRUCTURE of the two deals, requires no competitor rate data, cannot be refuted, and lands harder because the reader does the math themselves. Use this framing. Do NOT assert that renting costs more in dollars unless and until real rental rates are verified per company and dated.

REWORDING LINE 8 ALONE, AS INSTRUCTED, DROPPED IT TO 2 UNITS, SWALLOWING ALL EIGHT REAL LITERALS INTO TWO GIANT NON-ATOMIC BLOBS. That is total loss of coverage on the file's shipped copy, strictly worse than the status quo. Rewording all four gave exactly 8 units and nothing spurious. SO THE RULE IS: an EVEN number of stray quote characters in comments is benign, an ODD number is catastrophic and re-pairs every literal below the imbalance. Any future fix, guidance or lint rule must reason about PARITY across the whole scanned region, never about individual apostrophes. Advice of the form 'remove that apostrophe' is actively dangerous and the orchestrator gave exactly that advice. IMPLICATION FOR THE REAL FIX: stripping comments before extraction is still correct and is now clearly the ONLY safe fix, because any partial cleanup can flip parity and silently destroy coverage. A lint rule banning apostrophes in comments would also work but is strictly worse, since it fails open on the file someone edits without running it. IMPLICATION FOR T-036, SHARPER THAN BEFORE: a guard whose coverage silently inverts on the parity of punctuation in comments must not become a deploy gate until extractUnits ignores comments. The failure is not merely misdirection, it is that a well-intentioned cleanup commit can zero out scanning for a whole file while every test stays green. src/data/tools.ts now has all four comments reworded, zero comment apostrophes, and a new editing rule 4 mirroring the warning at src/pages/shipping-container-guides/index.astro:16. ||| DISPATCHED 2026-08-19 (resume session): astro-developer briefed to strip comments string-aware before extractUnits, add parity regression tests, fix the T-135 header comment in the same pass, and update the two stale in-file warnings. THE HARVEST'S MACHINE-READABLE SUMMARY IS UNRETRIEVABLE AFTER A RUN ENDS, and that is a diagnosability hole in the one system whose central design problem is telling 'nothing changed' apart from 'something broke quietly'. Found 2026-08-19 when the orchestrator asked for the summary line from the first production run and the agent COULD NOT PRODUCE IT, said so plainly, and supplied equivalent proof from the step log rather than paraphrasing a line it never had. That disclosure is the behaviour to reinforce. MECHANISM: the workflow redirects the script's stdout to $RUNNER_TEMP/harvest-summary.json, and $RUNNER_TEMP is discarded with the runner and is not uploaded as an artifact (artifacts.total_count 0). The $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY restatement is not exposed through the REST API either: the job check-run returns output.summary null and output.text null, and the internal summary_raw endpoints 404 even with a token. So the structured output of an unattended daily job exists nowhere retrievable once the run finishes. WHY IT MATTERS: debugging a run from three weeks ago gives you prose in the log and no JSON. The summary is the artifact that carries changeCount, the per-metro change list, warnings, failures, unsuppressed SKUs and the hysteresis state in a form that can be diffed or parsed. Losing it means every retrospective question gets answered by reading prose. FIX, small: `tee` the summary into $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY inside a fenced block, or upload it with actions/upload-artifact, or both. Prefer the artifact if retention matters, since step summaries are attached to the run and the artifact is downloadable and parseable. ALSO NOTED FROM THE SAME RUN, cosmetic today: actions/cache/restore@v4, actions/cache/save@v4, actions/checkout@v4 and actions/setup-node@v4 all target Node 20 and the runner is forcing them onto Node 24. This concerns the actions' own JS runtime, not the pinned Node 22, and it is what will eventually force a major bump on those four.
